AMELUMA PHOTO · INTERFACE AUDIT · 16 OCTOBER 2026

The photo should lead.
The interface should support it.

Ameluma has improved, but it does not yet have the consistent hierarchy, compact controls and predictable interaction of the reference applications. The next pass should consolidate the editing experience and recover canvas space before adding features.

Scope: macOS, iPadOS and iPhone. Reviewed current uncommitted source on HEAD 02078d3, including Retouch, Remove Watermark and Resize Quick Task changes. This is a review and action plan; no application code, signing, commit or push was changed during this audit.

EvidenceCompetitorsFindingsLayoutsAction planVerification

What this review actually establishes

Fresh native hierarchy captures were generated with synthetic local images through the existing review tests. iPad produced 37 attachments; iPhone 28. The Mac test produced 10 attachments before failing. Selected captures below were visually inspected. Generated fixtures expose layout and state combinations; they do not establish touch ergonomics, fluid animation, colour accuracy or successful first-time use.

The Mac captures are real current hosted views, but use a borderless test window: the app’s native title-bar toolbar is absent. Toolbar duplication findings are therefore source-confirmed, rather than measured from those screenshots. The Mac run failed with InvalidTransition { phase: idle, targetPhase: failed(deinit) } after the History capture; later Mac GIF/collage captures are unavailable in this pass. The cause remains unresolved.

Some iPad fixtures retain an open sidebar after earlier selection/navigation. Production code requests detail-only on entry to editing, and forces it while a drawing draft is open. These captures establish the cost when navigation is visible, not that every normal Editor launch shows it. Several fixtures also retain a rotated photo and a deliberately added black privacy mask. Those are intentional editing state, not rendering defects.

Competitor comparisons use current official documentation and published interface illustrations. Pixelmator Pro Mac/iPad and Photoshop iPhone illustrations were visually inspected. Photomator’s official interface, zoom and repair documentation was inspected; its image CDN returned HTTP 403, so this report does not claim a fresh Photomator screenshot inspection or hands-on competitor testing. Pixelmator Pro is compared on Mac/iPad; the phone comparison uses Photomator and Photoshop.

These products are references for hierarchy, not specifications to copy. Their screenshots use different image ratios, panel states and OS versions; a percentage ranking between these illustrations would be misleading. Pixelmator’s glass overlays can themselves obscure image detail, and Photoshop’s broad feature set can demand considerable navigation. Ameluma should retain an unobstructed safe working rectangle and a much smaller tool set.

Detailed findings and recommendations

P1 means a substantial task or working-space problem; P2 means consistency or finishing polish. “Confirmed” identifies source or capture evidence, not a claim of a live user study.

01 · Navigation consumes editing space P1

Confirmed: Mac navigation stays visible by default from 1,200 points wide, even in Editor. It reserves 220 points for workspace filters, workflows, presets and help while a single photo is being edited. iPad navigation can likewise coexist with tools and inspector; the portrait batch fixture spends roughly its left third on navigation. Unlike a layer panel, these controls rarely act on the current canvas.

Recommendation: Default to collapsed navigation during editing and creation. Keep a clear Workspace/back control and honour an explicit user preference. On iPad, treat the browser sidebar as temporary navigation. Keep it available for browsing and selecting inputs. Do not remove it globally or make people hunt for their photos.

Evidence: MacWorkspace; LibrarySidebar; EditorPanelLayout.navigationVisible; MobileWorkspace.

02 · Three rows precede the photo P1

Confirmed: Desktop Editor stacks document tabs, Workspace/previous/next/Original, then tool buttons. iPad normal Editor stacks tabs and a navigation/compare row beneath the native bar. Retouch uses a different header. Oversized tab padding and separately styled rows give navigation too much visual weight.

Recommendation: Keep one compact document strip and one action system. Move back/document identity, Undo/Redo, compare and Export into the native header where feasible. Use the adjacent tool rail on wide screens. Preserve the tabs, drag reordering, open-document chooser and close-without-deletion semantics.

03 · Inspector density varies dramatically P1

Confirmed: Mac adjustments show seven rows compactly; iPad compactPanel adjustment rows use much larger vertical spacing and fill most of the screen. Watermark uses a grouped form while Retouch and collage use custom rows. Each is native-looking individually, but they do not read as one designed product.

Recommendation: Standardise label/value/reset alignment, slider spacing and section hierarchy. Keep iPad touch regions at least 44 points, but avoid a separate tall row for every label and every slider. Initial design targets: roughly 40–48 points per desktop slider unit and 56–64 on default-size iPad; allow content and accessibility to expand. Use 8/12/16-point spacing tokens and right-aligned monospaced values. These are proposed budgets to validate, not competitor measurements.

04 · Undo is hidden in ordinary Editor P1

Confirmed: PhotoEditorWorkspace puts Undo and Redo in the Edits menu. Retouch, GIF and collage expose history differently. A person adjusting exposure must discover a menu for a basic safety action, despite the model already supporting it.

Recommendation: Give Undo/Redo a stable header location across tools. Bind them to the active editing context: draft stroke history during Retouch/Privacy/Annotate, photo history otherwise, composition history in creations. Keep descriptive history in the overflow menu and keyboard commands on Mac. Never visually unify buttons by accidentally unifying unrelated histories.

05 · Photo tools still feel like different editors P1

Confirmed: Mac switches from a horizontal full toolbox to a different left rail for overlay tools. On phone, Privacy/Annotate still use a scrolling controls-plus-canvas presentation; Retouch has a dedicated canvas-first layout. Draft tools also add a new Apply/Cancel footer.

Recommendation: Keep the same toolbox order, photo identity, canvas background and history position during every tool. Preserve explicit draft Apply/Cancel, with a small draft state indicator and the current guard against switching photos. First unify presentation and canvas sizing; do not rewrite the editing/session model or silently auto-apply drafts.

06 · iPhone prioritises Privacy over everyday tools P1

Confirmed: The permanent phone strip is Adjust, Crop, Privacy, Tools. Retouch, Resize, Annotate and Watermark are hidden in Tools. Home still lists Censor as a separate task and does not list Resize, even after the sidebar Quick Tasks update.

Recommendation: Use a small labelled strip such as Adjust, Crop, Retouch, Tools; keep Privacy readily visible within the toolbox. Put Convert and Resize together on Home. Remove Censor as a separate Home destination. All entries must reuse contextual photo selection and captured operation inputs. Validate the final default tool order with first-time users.

07 · Portrait options need adaptive size, not a fixed box P1

Confirmed: Ordinary iPad tool popovers are anchored correctly, but hard-code 320 × 440 points. Width and Dynamic Type can change while controls contain text fields, menus and instructions. A generic Done heading also takes space away from properties.

Recommendation: Size options to their content within available screen/keyboard bounds. Put mode and the most-used controls immediately under the active tool; keep precision fields in disclosures. Use a nonmodal adjacent pane where there is sufficient safe canvas, otherwise an anchored popover. Accessibility sizes should use a readable expanded presentation, not narrow multi-column controls.

08 · Canvas navigation changes meaning by tool P1

Confirmed: Normal editing offers “Inspect actual pixels” as a separate viewing mode. Overlay tools show a different zoom footer labelled “100% of fit”, with a 1–4× fit-relative zoom. Users cannot infer actual pixel magnification from that label.

Recommendation: Establish consistent Fit, 100% actual pixels, zoom and pan behaviour. Clearly distinguish viewport zoom from Crop zoom. Until actual-pixel magnification is implemented consistently, label fit-relative zoom as “1× fit”, not an ambiguous percentage. Support touch zoom without drawing a stroke and hardware keyboard/pointer navigation. Photomator’s documented zoom model is a useful reference.

09 · Batch selection and batch inputs look too similar P1

Confirmed: The iPad batch capture displays six selected thumbnails while the operation header says one photo; only one has a Batch input badge. These are deliberately distinct states, but blue selection styling makes it easy to assume all six will be changed.

Recommendation: Keep the stable captured operation scope and display it persistently: “Editing 1 photo · 6 selected in Workspace”. Use distinct marks for gallery selection and operation membership, plus a clear Change Photos command. Offer “Show operation photos” as a view choice. Do not solve the ambiguity by silently changing inputs when selection changes.

10 · Gallery header is still a control stack P2

Confirmed: Browse/Frame/Compare, Actions/Select/More, operation scope, processed-preview status, thumbnail size/reframing/history and search/filter occupy several rows before thumbnails. Common commands are intermixed with secondary view settings.

Recommendation: Keep one task row with scope and action menu, plus search/filter. Move thumbnail size and infrequent display options into View; put Frame guidance next to its toggle or show it once. Retain a visible hidden-selection count when filters are active. Keep this a workspace, not a photo-management dashboard.

11 · Export has competing homes P2

Confirmed: Mac photo/batch code includes an Export toolbar action and a large inspector footer. Output is also a tool. GIF and collage each introduce their own Export placement and labels.

Recommendation: Choose one primary Export action in the stable document header, with the output tool reserved for settings. Show photo/file count and destination in the export panel. Keep background progress and failures accessible in a compact status area. Preserve validated publication and successful-output-only sharing; reducing UI must not reduce these safeguards.

12 · Watermark removal was fixed; settings still need hierarchy P2

Confirmed: Remove Watermark now exists directly beneath the enabled switch and in the canvas context menu; percentage labels have been rounded. The fresh watermark fixture has watermark disabled, so it does not visually prove the enabled removal state. Source and the prior scoped Undo regression support the change.

Recommendation: When enabled, use a compact “Watermark · Remove” header rather than an Add toggle plus another large row. Expose content, size and opacity first. Group placement/rotation/tiling and presets under concise disclosures. Keep the explicit trash label; do not rely on a context menu as the sole removal route.

13 · GIF control stack outweighs its preview P1

Confirmed: The phone capture combines a second GIF heading, history/export, transport, frame selection/order, thumbnails, inspector tabs and a multi-row timing panel. The photo remains visible, but the working image is subordinate. A portrait canvas naturally needs side space; that is not a reason to crop it to fill the phone.

Recommendation: Keep transport and total duration on one row, one horizontally scrolling frame strip, and the active frame duration directly accessible. Put bulk timing, looping and canvas properties behind focused controls. Use an expandable drawer for detailed settings and retain the preview above it. Keep frame identities and selection semantics unchanged. Desktop should retain an efficient frame strip rather than gain a professional animation timeline.

14 · Collage navigation is redundant on phone P2

Confirmed: The fixture shows document title, Open Collages, Add Photos/More/Export, then Collage/Photo/Output and an Edit Collage launcher below the canvas. The bottom launcher mostly repeats the selected tab’s purpose.

Recommendation: Use one document menu in the header, one Export action, and contextual Canvas/Photo controls. On phone, tapping the selected control should open its drawer without another generic Edit button. On desktop, retain the recent aligned size row and compact appearance controls; do not revert to the old tall label stack.

15 · Large text passes visibility checks but remains awkward P1

Confirmed: The narrow iPad large-text fixture has a sidebar with words split across multiple lines and an oversized horizontal tool strip. The largest phone text fixture still displays the photo, but View/Edited/Edits/Tools consume substantial space. The capture test passing is not proof of accessible task completion.

Recommendation: At accessibility sizes, favour a single-column document area, a compact labelled tools menu and full-width readable forms. Keep navigation in a temporary presentation. Avoid repeated permanent status labels and fixed popover dimensions. Verify VoiceOver order, selected tool announcements, focus return and keyboard entry with real interaction.

16 · Small visual details still weaken the hierarchy P2

Confirmed: Tool selection uses different blue fills/tints across rails and menus. Mac photo tool buttons do not provide as strong a selected background as tablet buttons. Multiple More menus represent unrelated kinds of actions. “Individual Overrides” and “Inherits batch settings” expose the implementation model more than the task.

Recommendation: Standardise selected/disabled/hover/focus treatments, separators and icon sizes. Use familiar icons for repeat commands, but retain words for unfamiliar or destructive actions. Rename user-facing override summaries to “Photo-specific edits” or “Uses batch settings”, with details behind disclosure. Keep exact affected counts and review warnings visible. Provide help labels and accessible names for every icon.

Set aside a safe rectangle for the photo and fit the chosen output aspect ratio into it. Measure available canvas area separately from displayed photo area. Never stretch, crop or change output framing just to improve a screen-occupancy metric. A landscape photo on a portrait device will legitimately leave vertical room.

Implementation plan and acceptance gates

  1. Navigation and safety actions. Align iPhone Home with Convert/Resize and Editor-based Privacy. Make Undo/Redo consistently visible and remove redundant Export emphasis. Default navigation closed while editing, respecting deliberate user choice. Verify task-first/photo-first selection, cancel/return, captured input counts, tab switching and draft guards.
  2. Shared visual rules. Establish focused presentation components for row layout, section headings, document actions and tool selection. Start with Adjust and Watermark, then apply to Retouch and creation controls. Avoid a broad coordinator rewrite. Verify light/dark, numeric keyboard, focus, mixed values, sparse patches and Undo grouping.
  3. Stable photo editing workspace. Keep the toolbox and canvas shell consistent while Privacy/Annotate/Retouch retain their transactional state. Improve portrait option sizing and unify viewport zoom semantics. Check source picking, drawing versus panning, brush preview, remove/restore, apply/discard and tool switching.
  4. GIF, collage and batch compression. Reduce duplicate headers, group frame/creation controls and distinguish selected photos from captured inputs. Reuse presentation rules, not a new composition engine. Check frame identities/order/timing, saved creations, missing-source recovery and unchanged output.
  5. Interaction and physical-device review. Run a repeatable task matrix with realistic landscape, portrait, square and panoramic images. Compare before/after at the same size and state. Cover iPhone portrait/landscape, small phone, 11/13-inch iPad, narrow multitasking, large text, Mac narrow/wide windows, keyboard, pointer and Pencil. Perform novice task walkthroughs before declaring the polish complete.

Specific acceptance criteria: Undo requires no menu in normal editing; active tool and operation count remain visible; non-draft editing uses one primary document action header and at most one document strip; tool options originate beside their trigger; common controls do not require scrolling past help/presets; no clipped value, action or unexplained disabled control; navigation and selection changes never change captured operation inputs; closing options increases usable canvas without discarding state.

Proposed space budgets: Mac tool rail 36–44 points, inspector initially 280–320; iPad tool rail 48–56, inspector initially 280–320 only when the remaining canvas is useful; phone property drawer collapsible to its selected control. These are starting specifications, not fixed limits. Accessibility and input needs take precedence. Record safe canvas dimensions, actual aspect-fit image dimensions and interaction occlusion before and after; avoid a single arbitrary “photo percentage” pass score.

Preserve shared rendering, source snapshots, project formats, sparse inheritance, separate selection/operation/frame identities, draft safety, validation and local-only processing. This work should not add layers, complex docking, new editing tools or photo-management features.
